definition: A clear question that the study is designed to answer and that is narrow enough for the chosen methods.
wrongs: A broad topic title with no question the study could answer.
The list of references at the end of a paper.
The researcher's personal hope that the result will be interesting.
why: A research question states what the study will answer and guides the choice of method and data.
example: The study asks whether a two-minute video guide reduces password-reset calls among first-year students.
scenario: A proposal has only the title student passwords and no question the data could answer. What must be added before the method can be chosen?
scenarioWrongs: A longer topic title and nothing else
The reference list from another paper
A statement that the result should be interesting
scenarioWhy: Methods are chosen to answer a research question, so a topic title alone is not enough.

definition: A specific outcome the study intends to achieve, written so a reader can tell when it has been met.
wrongs: A slogan such as explore the area, with no checkable outcome.
The name of the statistics package.
The word count of the report.
why: An objective is a concrete outcome of the study, specific enough that completion can be judged.
example: One objective is to measure the change in reset calls in the month after the video guide is published.
scenario: The proposal says explore passwords. Reviewers cannot tell when the study would be finished. Which replacement is a research objective?
scenarioAnswer: Measure the change in reset calls one month after the guide
scenarioWrongs: Explore the area of passwords
Use a well-known statistics package
Reach a preferred word count
scenarioWhy: A research objective states a checkable outcome, such as measuring a defined change.

definition: A critical synthesis of published work that shows what is already known and where the new study fits.
wrongs: A list of quotations placed one after another with no comparison or argument.
The raw data tables from the author's own new experiment.
A bibliography that names sources but never discusses them.
why: A literature review argues from existing work; it is more than a sequence of summaries or a bare list of titles.
example: A chapter compares three studies of password videos, notes their conflicting results, and identifies the missing student-call measure.
scenario: A draft lists twenty quotations in date order and never compares them. Which improvement would make it a literature review?
scenarioAnswer: Synthesise the sources into an argument about what is known and missing
scenarioWrongs: Add more quotations and still not compare them
Replace the chapter with the new experiment's raw tables
Leave a list of titles with no discussion
scenarioWhy: A literature review critically synthesises sources to show the state of knowledge and the gap.

definition: A reference that identifies the source of an idea, quotation, figure, or finding used in the work.
wrongs: A decorative footnote that points to no real source.
Changing a few words so the source need not be named.
A compliment paid to the supervisor in the acknowledgements.
why: A citation tells the reader exactly which source supports a borrowed idea or result.
example: A sentence about reset-call rates ends with an author-year citation that matches an entry in the reference list.
scenario: You use another study's finding about reset calls in your introduction. Which addition gives the reader the source?
scenarioAnswer: A citation that identifies that study
scenarioWrongs: A footnote that names no source
A wording tweak so the source can be hidden
A thank-you to the supervisor
scenarioWhy: A citation identifies the source of the finding so the reader can trace it.

definition: A publication that experts in the field have examined for quality before it was accepted.
wrongs: Any page that appears near the top of a general web search.
An anonymous blog post with no editorial checks.
An advertisement written by the product's vendor.
why: Peer review means qualified reviewers assessed the work before publication, which is a quality filter, not a guarantee.
example: The student prefers a journal article on training videos that independent reviewers accepted over a vendor's blog.
scenario: You need a quality-checked study of training videos rather than a vendor advert. Which source type fits?
scenarioWrongs: The first web hit with no review
An anonymous unchecked blog
The vendor's advertisement
scenarioWhy: A peer-reviewed article has been examined by field experts before acceptance.

definition: Original research or firsthand evidence, such as a paper in which the authors report a study they conducted.
wrongs: A textbook chapter that only summarises other people's studies.
A news story that retells a journal article.
A lecture slide that cites a review paper.
why: A primary source presents original evidence, whereas secondary sources interpret or summarise that evidence.
example: The student reads the original experiment on video guides rather than only the textbook paragraph about it.
scenario: You need the authors' own report of their video-guide experiment, not a retelling. Which source should you read?
scenarioWrongs: A textbook summary of that paper
A news retelling
A slide that cites a review
scenarioWhy: The paper in which the authors report their own study is the primary source.

definition: A work that summarises, reviews, or interprets primary research rather than reporting a new study by its author.
wrongs: The dataset collected by the original experimenters.
A lab notebook from the study itself.
The patent filed by the people who ran the trial.
why: A secondary source comments on or synthesises primary work; it is not the original evidence.
example: A review article compares twelve password studies but does not itself run a new experiment.
scenario: An article compares twelve studies and runs no new experiment. Which label fits that article?
scenarioWrongs: The original experimenters' dataset
A lab notebook from one of the trials
The inventors' patent on a new device
scenarioWhy: A review that interprets other studies, without a new study, is a secondary source.

definition: An unanswered or weakly supported question in the literature that a new study can justifiably address.
wrongs: A topic that many recent studies have already settled with consistent evidence.
A spelling mistake in one old paper.
The researcher's dislike of a previous author's writing style.
why: A research gap is a genuine opening in what is known, which justifies a new study.
example: Studies measure exam scores after a video, but none measure whether help-desk calls actually fall.
scenario: Many papers agree on exam scores after training videos, but none measure help-desk calls. Which opening can justify a new study?
scenarioAnswer: The unmeasured effect on help-desk calls
scenarioWrongs: A result that recent studies have already settled
A spelling mistake in an old paper
Dislike of an author's style
scenarioWhy: A research gap is an unanswered question, here the effect on help-desk calls.

definition: A set of established theories used to explain the phenomenon and to guide what the study examines.
wrongs: The researcher's informal hunch with no link to established theory.
The spreadsheet layout used to store responses.
The ethics form's contact details.
why: A theoretical framework uses existing theory to explain the phenomenon and shape the study.
example: The study uses cognitive load theory to explain why a short video might beat a long written policy.
scenario: You explain the expected benefit of a short video by using cognitive load theory. Which role is that theory playing?
scenarioWrongs: An unsupported personal hunch
The spreadsheet layout
The ethics form's phone number
scenarioWhy: Using an established theory to explain and guide the study makes it the theoretical framework.

definition: The researcher's description or diagram of the concepts in the study and the expected links among them.
wrongs: A named body of established theory adopted without showing the study's own concepts.
The consent form signed by participants.
The printer driver used to produce the diagram.
why: A conceptual framework shows how this study's concepts are expected to relate, often in a diagram.
example: A diagram links video length to understanding and then to the number of reset calls.
scenario: A diagram shows video length affecting understanding, which then affects reset calls. Which artefact is that diagram?
scenarioWrongs: A consent form
A printer driver
A theory name with no concepts from this study
scenarioWhy: A diagram of this study's concepts and expected links is the conceptual framework.

definition: A testable statement that predicts a relationship or difference between variables.
wrongs: A question that does not predict what will be found.
A moral judgement that cannot be tested with data.
A description of the sample size.
why: A hypothesis predicts an observable relationship or difference so that data can support or contradict it.
example: The hypothesis states that students given the short video will make fewer reset calls than those given the policy text.
scenario: You predict that the video group will log fewer reset calls than the text group. Which kind of statement is that prediction?
scenarioWrongs: A question with no predicted outcome
A moral claim that data cannot test
The planned sample size
scenarioWhy: A testable prediction of a difference between groups is a hypothesis.

definition: A statement, used for statistical testing, that there is no effect or no difference in the population.
wrongs: The prediction that the treatment group will do better than the control group.
The research question written as a sentence.
The conclusion the author hopes reviewers will like.
why: The null hypothesis states no effect or no difference and is the statement the test attempts to reject.
example: The null states that mean reset calls do not differ between the video group and the text group.
scenario: The test assumes no difference in mean reset calls between the two groups. Which statement is that?
scenarioWrongs: The prediction that video is better
The research question
The conclusion the author prefers
scenarioWhy: A statement of no difference, used as the basis of the test, is the null hypothesis.

definition: A statement that there is an effect or a difference, considered if the evidence leads you to reject the null.
wrongs: The statement that there is no effect in the population.
A description of how the sample was recruited.
The list of variables with no predicted effect.
why: The alternative hypothesis states that an effect or difference exists and is adopted only if the null is rejected.
example: The alternative states that mean reset calls differ between students who saw the video and those who read the text.
scenario: You will claim a difference in mean calls only if the test rejects no difference. Which statement expresses that difference?
scenarioWrongs: The statement of no effect
The recruitment method
A variable list with no predicted effect
scenarioWhy: The statement that a difference exists is the alternative hypothesis.

definition: The variable that the researcher changes or groups by, in order to examine its relationship with an outcome.
wrongs: The outcome that is measured to see whether it changes.
A factor deliberately held constant so it cannot explain the result.
The name of the ethics committee.
why: The independent variable is the presumed influence or grouping, not the measured outcome.
example: The study assigns students to either a short video or a text policy, which is the independent variable.
scenario: Students are assigned either a video or a text, and reset calls are counted afterwards. Which is the independent variable?
scenarioAnswer: The guide type, video or text
scenarioWrongs: The number of reset calls
The classroom, which is kept the same
The name of the ethics committee
scenarioWhy: The factor the researcher assigns, the type of guide, is the independent variable.

definition: The outcome variable that is measured to see whether it is associated with, or affected by, the independent variable.
wrongs: The condition the researcher assigns to participants.
A factor held constant throughout the study.
The software brand used to draw a chart.
why: The dependent variable is the measured outcome, not the condition the researcher manipulates.
example: The number of password-reset calls in the following month is the dependent variable.
scenario: Guide type is assigned, and the study counts reset calls over the next month. Which is the dependent variable?
scenarioWrongs: Whether the student saw video or text
The week of term, which was held constant
The chart software
scenarioWhy: The measured outcome, reset calls, is the dependent variable.

definition: A factor that is held constant or accounted for so it does not distort the relationship being studied.
wrongs: The outcome the study measures.
The condition that is deliberately varied between groups.
A factor left free to differ even though it could explain the result.
why: A control variable is managed so that it cannot offer an alternative explanation of the outcome.
example: Both groups use the same help-desk and the same week of term so those factors cannot explain a difference in calls.
scenario: Both groups share the same help-desk and the same week so those factors cannot explain the result. What role do those factors play?
scenarioWrongs: Dependent variables
Independent variables that were varied
Factors left free to confound the result
scenarioWhy: Factors held constant so they cannot explain the outcome are control variables.

definition: A statement of how a concept will be observed or measured in a particular study.
wrongs: A dictionary definition that never says how this study will measure the concept.
The researcher's private feeling about the concept.
The title of the statistics textbook.
why: An operational definition makes a concept measurable by stating the exact observation this study will use.
example: Understanding is operationalised as the score on a ten-item quiz taken immediately after the guide.
scenario: The study must say exactly how understanding will be measured. Which statement is an operational definition?
scenarioAnswer: The score on a ten-item quiz taken right after the guide
scenarioWrongs: A dictionary sentence that sets no measure
The researcher's feeling that students understood
The title of a statistics book
scenarioWhy: An operational definition states the concrete measurement used in this study.

definition: The full set of people, items, or events about which the study aims to draw a conclusion.
wrongs: The subset that is actually measured.
The list used to draw the sample, if that list omits part of the group of interest.
The number of questions on the questionnaire.
why: The population is the entire group the conclusions are meant to cover, not only those who were observed.
example: The population is all first-year undergraduates at the university, not only the 200 who answered the survey.
scenario: Conclusions are meant to cover every first-year student, but only 200 answer. Which group is the population?
scenarioAnswer: All first-year undergraduates at the university
scenarioWrongs: The 200 who answered
The questionnaire's question count
Only students who happened to be in one cafe
scenarioWhy: The population is the full set the study wants to conclude about, here every first-year student.

definition: The subset of the population that is actually observed or measured in the study.
wrongs: The entire population, including people who were never contacted.
The sampling method's name, rather than the people selected.
The hypothesis being tested.
why: The sample is the part of the population from which data are actually collected.
example: Of all first-year students, the 200 who completed the quiz form the sample.
scenario: Data come from 200 first-year students, not from every first-year student. Which group is the sample?
scenarioWrongs: Every first-year student, including those not contacted
The name of the sampling method
The hypothesis
scenarioWhy: The sample is the subset that was actually observed.

definition: The list or other representation of the population from which the sample is actually drawn.
wrongs: The people who end up in the final dataset.
The theoretical population, including people missing from every available list.
The questionnaire itself.
why: The sampling frame is the operational list used for selection and may not perfectly match the population.
example: The frame is the registrar's enrolment list, which omits two late-joining students.
scenario: Names are drawn from the registrar's enrolment list, which misses late joiners. Which item is the sampling frame?
scenarioWrongs: Only the students who already replied
The ideal population including people on no list
The questionnaire
scenarioWhy: The list from which the sample is drawn is the sampling frame.

definition: A probability method in which every member of the frame has an equal chance of being included.
wrongs: Picking whoever is easiest to reach in a corridor.
Choosing people because they volunteered after an advert.
Taking every person from only one convenient class.
why: Simple random sampling gives each member of the frame an equal chance of selection.
example: A program draws 200 names at random from the full enrolment list, each student having an equal chance.
scenario: Each student on the enrolment list must have the same chance of selection. Which method fits?
scenarioWrongs: Asking whoever walks past
Taking only volunteers from an advert
Using one convenient class in full
scenarioWhy: Equal chance of selection for every member of the frame is simple random sampling.

definition: A method that divides the population into subgroups and then draws a sample from each subgroup.
wrongs: Drawing names from the whole list with no subgroups.
Choosing the easiest people regardless of subgroup.
Letting one subgroup stand in for all the others.
why: Stratified sampling samples within defined subgroups so those subgroups are represented.
example: The frame is split into faculties, and a random sample is drawn inside each faculty.
scenario: Each faculty must be represented, so names are drawn at random inside every faculty. Which method is that?
scenarioWrongs: One simple random draw with no faculty split
Picking the easiest students only
Surveying a single faculty and ignoring the rest
scenarioWhy: Dividing into subgroups and sampling from each one is stratified sampling.

definition: A non-probability method that selects whoever is easiest to reach, which limits how far results can be generalised.
wrongs: A method in which every member of the frame has an equal chance.
A method that samples randomly inside every important subgroup.
A census that measures the entire population.
why: Convenience sampling trades representativeness for ease, so generalisation is weak.
example: The researcher surveys students who happen to be in the library on a Tuesday afternoon.
scenario: You survey only students sitting in the library on Tuesday because they are easy to reach. Which method is that?
scenarioWrongs: Simple random sampling from the full list
Random draws inside every faculty
A census of all students
scenarioWhy: Selecting whoever is easiest to reach is convenience sampling and limits generalisation.

definition: The number of observations included in the study, which affects precision and the ability to detect an effect.
wrongs: The number of questions on the form, if each person answers once.
The size of the population the study hopes to talk about.
The number of authors on the paper.
why: Sample size is how many observations are analysed, and larger samples usually give more precise estimates.
example: The study analyses quiz scores from 180 students, so the sample size is 180.
scenario: Quiz scores from 180 students will be analysed, one score each. Which number is the sample size?
scenarioWrongs: The 10 questions on the quiz
The 4,000 students in the population
The 2 authors of the report
scenarioWhy: Sample size is the number of observations, here the 180 student scores.

definition: A systematic error that pushes results away from the true value, rather than random variation around it.
wrongs: Chance differences that average out as more data are collected.
A clearly reported limitation that does not shift the estimate.
The use of a random sample from a complete frame.
why: Bias is systematic: it pushes the result in a direction, unlike random error that varies around the truth.
example: Only students who loved the video reply, so the measured satisfaction is higher than the true class value.
scenario: Only students who loved the video reply, and satisfaction looks higher than it is for the class. Which problem is that?
scenarioWrongs: Random variation that would shrink with more replies
A random sample from a complete list
A limitation that does not move the estimate
scenarioWhy: A systematic push away from the true value, here from who chooses to reply, is bias.

definition: The extent to which a study supports a causal conclusion in its own setting, rather than a result caused by a confound.
wrongs: The extent to which the finding applies to other universities and years.
The consistency of a questionnaire when it is repeated.
The number of references in the literature chapter.
why: Internal validity concerns whether the study itself can support a cause-and-effect claim.
example: Because both groups share the same week and help-desk, a drop in calls is more plausibly due to the video.
scenario: A critic says a holiday week, not the video, caused fewer calls. Which property is being challenged?
scenarioWrongs: Whether the result applies to other universities
Whether the quiz gives the same score twice
The length of the reference list
scenarioWhy: A possible confound attacks internal validity, the basis for a causal claim inside the study.

definition: The extent to which findings can be generalised to other people, settings, or times.
wrongs: Whether the study's own design rules out confounds.
Whether a scale produces the same score on a retest.
Whether the null hypothesis was rejected.
why: External validity is about generalisation beyond the people and setting actually studied.
example: A result from one small private college may not generalise to a large public university.
scenario: The result comes from one small college, and you ask whether it applies to large public universities. Which property is that question about?
scenarioWrongs: Whether a confound explains the college result
Whether the quiz is stable on retest
Whether the p-value was below 0.05
scenarioWhy: Generalising beyond the studied setting is a question of external validity.

definition: The extent to which a measure actually captures the concept it is intended to represent.
wrongs: Whether the sample can be generalised to another country.
Whether two groups were assigned fairly.
Whether the paper was peer reviewed.
why: Construct validity asks if the measurement matches the concept, not if the sample generalises.
example: A quiz of trivia about the video's actors is a poor measure of the concept password-reset skill.
scenario: The quiz asks about the presenter's clothes, but the concept is password-reset skill. Which property is weak?
scenarioWrongs: Generalisation to another country
Fairness of random assignment
Whether reviewers accepted the paper
scenarioWhy: Construct validity is weak when the measure does not capture the intended concept.

definition: The consistency of a measure when it is repeated under the same conditions.
wrongs: Proof that the measure captures the right concept.
Proof that the result applies to every university.
Proof that one variable causes another.
why: Reliability means consistency of measurement; a measure can be consistent and still measure the wrong concept.
example: Students who retake the same quiz under the same conditions receive nearly the same scores.
scenario: The same students retake the same quiz under the same conditions and scores barely change. Which property does that support?
scenarioWrongs: Proof the quiz measures the intended concept
Proof the result applies worldwide
Proof that the video causes fewer calls
scenarioWhy: Similar scores on repetition support reliability, which is consistency, not correctness of the concept.

definition: Research that collects numerical data and uses statistical analysis to test relationships or differences.
wrongs: Research that interprets interviews and documents without numerical testing.
A literature review that includes no new data.
A project diary written only in prose.
why: Quantitative research uses numbers and statistics to examine relationships or group differences.
example: The study compares mean reset-call counts between two groups with a statistical test.
scenario: You will compare mean call counts between two groups with a statistical test. Which approach is that?
scenarioWrongs: Interpreting interviews with no numerical test
A literature review with no new data
A prose diary of the project
scenarioWhy: Collecting numerical data and testing a difference statistically is quantitative research.

definition: Research that collects non-numerical data, such as interviews or documents, to interpret meanings and experiences.
wrongs: Research whose main analysis is a statistical test of numerical group differences.
A census that only counts people.
A calculation of a mean and a standard deviation alone.
why: Qualitative research interprets meanings in non-numerical material such as talk or text.
example: Students are interviewed about why they ignore password prompts, and themes are coded from the transcripts.
scenario: You interview students about why they ignore prompts and code themes from the transcripts. Which approach is that?
scenarioWrongs: A statistical test of two mean scores
A census that only counts people
Computing a mean and standard deviation only
scenarioWhy: Interpreting interview meanings through themes is qualitative research.

definition: Numerical summaries, such as averages and spreads, that describe the data actually collected.
wrongs: Tests that use a sample to draw a conclusion about a wider population.
The ethical rules for recruiting participants.
The sampling method's name.
why: Descriptive statistics summarise the observed data and do not, by themselves, infer beyond that data.
example: The report states that the 180 quiz scores have a mean of 7.4 and a standard deviation of 1.2.
scenario: You report the mean and spread of the 180 scores you collected, with no claim about all students. Which statistics are those?
scenarioWrongs: A test used to infer a population effect
The ethics rules
The name of the sampling method
scenarioWhy: Summaries of the data in hand, such as mean and spread, are descriptive statistics.

definition: Methods that use sample data to draw conclusions about a larger population, including estimates and hypothesis tests.
wrongs: Summaries that describe only the observed scores and make no population claim.
The consent statement read to participants.
A diagram of the concepts with no data.
why: Inferential statistics go beyond the sample to estimate or test claims about a population.
example: A test uses the sample of 180 students to judge whether video and text differ in the whole first-year population.
scenario: The sample is used to judge whether video and text differ for all first-year students. Which methods do that?
scenarioWrongs: A mean that describes only the sample
The consent statement
A concept diagram with no data
scenarioWhy: Using sample data to conclude about a larger population is inferential statistics.

definition: The arithmetic average of a set of numbers, found by dividing their sum by how many values there are.
wrongs: The middle value when the numbers are ordered.
The most frequently occurring value.
The difference between the largest and smallest values.
why: The mean is the sum of the values divided by the count of values.
example: Scores of 6, 7, and 8 have a mean of 7 because their sum is 21 and there are three scores.
scenario: Three quiz scores are 6, 7, and 8. Which value is their mean?
scenarioWhy: The mean is the sum divided by the count: 21 divided by 3 equals 7.

definition: A measure of how far values in a data set typically sit from their mean.
wrongs: The arithmetic average of the values.
The middle value of the ordered list.
The probability of the data given the null hypothesis.
why: Standard deviation summarises typical distance from the mean, so it describes spread rather than centre.
example: Two classes both average 70, but the class with scores tightly clustered has the smaller standard deviation.
scenario: Two classes share a mean of 70, but one class's scores cluster tightly and the other's are widely spread. Which measure shows that difference?
scenarioWrongs: The mean, which is the same
The middle name of the teacher
The p-value of an unrelated test
scenarioWhy: Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean, so it distinguishes the tight and wide classes.

definition: A range computed from a sample that, under the method's assumptions, would cover the true population value in a stated percentage of repeated samples.
wrongs: The probability that this particular interval already calculated is the only correct one in a personal sense.
The range from the smallest to the largest raw observation, with no inferential claim.
The set of all values the researcher would prefer to see.
why: A confidence interval is an inferential range for a population value, with a stated confidence level tied to the method.
example: From the sample, the 95 percent confidence interval for the mean score runs from 7.1 to 7.7.
scenario: A sample produces a 95 percent interval of 7.1 to 7.7 for the population mean score. Which result is that interval?
scenarioWrongs: The range of the raw scores only
The values the researcher hopes for
The standard deviation of the sample
scenarioWhy: A range estimated from the sample for a population value, at a stated confidence level, is a confidence interval.

definition: The probability of data at least as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis were true.
wrongs: The probability that the null hypothesis itself is true.
The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true.
The size of the effect in practical units.
why: A p-value is computed assuming the null is true; it is not the probability that the null is true.
example: If there were truly no group difference, data this extreme would occur with probability 0.03, so the p-value is 0.03.
scenario: A classmate says the p-value of 0.03 is the probability that the null hypothesis is true. Which correction is right?
scenarioAnswer: It is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null were true
scenarioWrongs: It is the probability that the null is true
It is the probability that the alternative is true
It is the practical size of the call-rate difference
scenarioWhy: The p-value assumes the null is true and states how surprising the data would then be.

definition: A result unlikely under the null hypothesis at a pre-set threshold, treated as evidence against that null.
wrongs: A result that is automatically large enough to matter in practice.
Proof that the null hypothesis is false beyond any doubt.
A finding that must be true of every future sample.
why: Statistical significance means the result is unlikely given the null and the chosen threshold; it is not practical importance.
example: With a threshold of 0.05, a p-value of 0.03 is reported as statistically significant.
scenario: The threshold was set at 0.05 and the p-value is 0.03. Which claim is justified by that comparison alone?
scenarioWrongs: The effect is certainly important in practice
The null is impossible
Every future sample will match this one
scenarioWhy: A p-value below the pre-set threshold supports calling the result statistically significant, not practically important.

definition: Rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true, also called a false positive.
wrongs: Failing to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false.
Measuring the spread of a sample.
Choosing a sample that is too convenient.
why: A Type I error is a false claim of an effect when the null is true.
example: The groups do not truly differ, but the test rejects the null and the report claims a difference.
scenario: There is truly no difference, yet the test rejects the null and a difference is claimed. Which error is that?
scenarioWrongs: A Type II error
A calculation of the standard deviation
The use of a convenience sample
scenarioWhy: Rejecting a true null is a Type I error, a false positive.

definition: Failing to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false, also called a false negative.
wrongs: Rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true.
Reporting a confidence interval correctly.
Citing the source of a statistic.
why: A Type II error misses a real effect by failing to reject a false null.
example: The video truly reduces calls, but a tiny sample does not reject the null, so the report finds no difference.
scenario: The video truly reduces calls, but the test does not reject no difference. Which error is that?
scenarioWrongs: A Type I error
A correctly reported confidence interval
A proper citation
scenarioWhy: Failing to reject a false null is a Type II error, a false negative.

definition: A statistical association in which two variables vary together, which by itself does not prove that one causes the other.
wrongs: Proof that changing one variable will produce a change in the other.
A difference between the means of two experimentally assigned groups.
The ethical approval number of a study.
why: Correlation describes association; causation needs a design that can support a causal claim.
example: Hours of video watched and quiz scores rise together, but the study did not assign the hours.
scenario: Video hours and quiz scores rise together, and nothing was assigned by the researcher. Which claim is justified?
scenarioWrongs: Watching more video causes the higher scores
The means of two randomised groups differ
The study has ethical approval because of the association
scenarioWhy: Joint variation without a causal design supports correlation, not causation.

definition: A relationship in which a change in one variable produces a change in another, supported by design rather than by association alone.
wrongs: Any correlation, which is enough on its own to prove cause.
Two variables that were measured at the same time with no attempt to rule out other explanations.
A significant p-value from a convenience sample with obvious confounds.
why: A causal claim needs a design, such as controlled assignment, that can rule out alternative explanations.
example: Students are randomly assigned to video or text, and other conditions are held constant, before calls are compared.
scenario: You want to claim the video produces fewer calls, not merely that the two are associated. Which design feature is required?
scenarioAnswer: A design that rules out alternative explanations, such as random assignment
scenarioWrongs: A correlation by itself
Measuring both variables once with no controls
A small p-value from a confounded convenience sample
scenarioWhy: Causation requires a design that can support a production claim, not association alone.

definition: Voluntary agreement to take part, given after the person understands the purpose, procedures, risks, and right to withdraw.
wrongs: A requirement to participate because the person is enrolled in a class.
A signature collected with no explanation of the study.
Consent given by the researcher on the participant's behalf.
why: Research consent is informed and voluntary, and it includes the freedom to withdraw.
example: Before interviews, students read a sheet on recording, anonymity, and withdrawal, and then sign if they agree.
scenario: You want to interview students. Which step secures research informed consent?
scenarioAnswer: Explain purpose, risks, and withdrawal, then accept only voluntary agreement
scenarioWrongs: Require participation because they are in the class
Collect a signature with no explanation
Sign the form yourself for them
scenarioWhy: Informed consent is a voluntary agreement after the participant understands the study and the right to withdraw.

definition: Principles that protect participants and the integrity of a study, including consent, avoidance of harm, and honesty.
wrongs: A rule that interesting results justify hiding risks from participants.
A requirement to fabricate data if the hypothesis looks weak.
A ban on telling participants they may withdraw.
why: Research ethics protect people and require honest conduct; they are not waived for an interesting result.
example: A study of staff passwords is redesigned so it does not collect live passwords, after ethics review flags the harm.
scenario: A design would collect live staff passwords and cannot explain a matching benefit. Which demand of research ethics applies?
scenarioAnswer: Change the design to avoid unjustified harm
scenarioWrongs: Hide the risk because the result would be interesting
Invent safer-looking data
Forbid participants to withdraw
scenarioWhy: Research ethics require avoidance of unjustified harm, so the dangerous design must change.

definition: A condition in which the researcher cannot link a response to the identity of the person who provided it.
wrongs: A promise to store names securely while the researcher still knows who answered.
Using first names in a published transcript.
Collecting student IDs on every questionnaire.
why: Anonymity means even the researcher cannot connect responses to identities, which is stronger than confidential storage of names.
example: Questionnaires are returned with no name or ID, and the researcher has no key that could reconnect them.
scenario: You must ensure that even you cannot tell who gave which quiz sheet. Which condition are you creating?
scenarioWrongs: Confidential storage of a name list you can still match
Publishing first names
Printing student IDs on every sheet
scenarioWhy: Anonymity means responses cannot be linked to identities, including by the researcher.

definition: The duty to protect participants' identities and data from unauthorised disclosure, even when the researcher knows who they are.
wrongs: A design in which nobody, including the researcher, can ever match a response to a person.
A right to publish names because the findings are useful.
Storing consent forms and named transcripts on a public website.
why: Confidentiality protects known identities from disclosure; it is different from anonymity, where identities are not known.
example: Interview names are kept in a locked file separate from transcripts and are not used in the thesis.
scenario: You know who was interviewed and must stop others identifying them in the thesis. Which duty is that?
scenarioWrongs: Anonymity, which you no longer have because you know the names
A right to publish the names
Uploading named transcripts to a public site
scenarioWhy: Protecting identities you do know from unauthorised disclosure is confidentiality.

definition: Making up data or results and reporting them as if they had been collected.
wrongs: Excluding a pre-stated outlier using a rule written before the data were seen.
Reporting a non-significant result honestly.
Citing a source you actually read.
why: Fabrication is invention of data or results, which is research misconduct.
example: A student who lost the questionnaires types plausible scores and presents them as real responses.
scenario: The questionnaires were lost, so a student types plausible scores and treats them as real. Which misconduct is that?
scenarioWrongs: Applying a pre-stated outlier rule
Reporting a non-significant result
Citing a source that was read
scenarioWhy: Inventing data and reporting them as collected is fabrication.

definition: Manipulating research materials, equipment, or data so that the reported record misrepresents the study.
wrongs: Inventing an entire dataset that was never collected.
Correcting a typo in a transcription and noting the correction.
Analysing the data with the test named in the proposal.
why: Falsification changes real materials or data so the report no longer represents what happened.
example: A student deletes the questionnaires that contradict the hypothesis and analyses only the rest, without saying so.
scenario: Real questionnaires that contradict the hypothesis are deleted and the deletion is hidden. Which misconduct is that?
scenarioWrongs: Inventing a dataset that never existed
Noting a transcription typo that was fixed
Using the statistical test named in the proposal
scenarioWhy: Altering the real data record so it misrepresents the study is falsification.

definition: Using another person's words, ideas, or data without proper credit and presenting that material as your own.
wrongs: Quoting a source with quotation marks and a matching citation.
Paraphrasing an idea and citing the source.
Reporting data you collected yourself.
why: Plagiarism presents someone else's work as yours; quotation or paraphrase with credit avoids it.
example: A method section copies a paper's procedure paragraph and does not cite that paper.
scenario: A procedure paragraph is copied from a paper and no source is given. Which label fits the draft?
scenarioWrongs: A quotation with marks and a citation
A paraphrase that cites the source
A report of data you collected
scenarioWhy: Copying another's words into the thesis without credit is plagiarism.

definition: A structured account of a study that states the question, method, results, and interpretation so others can evaluate it.
wrongs: A press release that gives only a slogan and no method.
The raw data file with no explanation.
An ethics application written before any results exist.
why: A research report lets others judge the study by presenting question, method, results, and interpretation together.
example: The paper states the call-rate question, how groups were assigned, the test result, and what that result means.
scenario: Readers must be able to judge how the call-rate question was studied and what was found. Which document does that?
scenarioWrongs: A slogan-only press release
A raw data file with no explanation
The ethics form written before the results
scenarioWhy: A research report presents the question, method, results, and interpretation for evaluation.
